content.text: The problem appears to be a character encoding issue:  if you remove the inverted exclamation point from the
value of the test bibframe record in the integration test, the test then passes on Windows.  Put it back in, and the test fails.
I'll look into this more:  as far as I can tell, that character is a valid UTF-8 character.
The problem is the default platform encoding:
Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: Cp1252
We shouldn't really ever be using default platform encoding, we should explicitly call out UTF-8 via
. He wrote, knowing that he rarely does that.
Should that be built into the test?  or into the server that handles the PUT request?
The quickest-and-dirtiest approach to fixing the test is to remove the inverted exclamation mark.  I'm okay with that, since it is a bibframe test, not a character-encoding test.

That said, I'm wondering about character encoding issues out in the wild, and how to handle those gracefully.  At the very least, shouldn't the server detect if there's an encoding mismatch, and return something a bit more enlightening than a  java.nio.charset.MalformedInputException?  I'm thinking it may make more sense to fix this test, then open up an enhancement ticket for later on, to gracefully deal with encoding issues, complete with some sample curl transactions to test the behavior (later to be fleshed out as character encoding integration tests).

code, I should think). Everything flowing in after the HTTP machinery should be UTF-8. That's how we get rid of this nonsense once and for all. I think we could do something here with JAX-RS machinery to ensure it.

I take your point about the test in question being about Bibframe, but ironically, library metadata is an oozing, crusty pit full of badly-formed characters washing around in a greasy puddle of XML that lies about its own encoding. It's probably where this kind of problem would first appear, anyway.

Yeah, I agree, which is why I'm for testing server-side content charset validation in its own set of IT tests, not mixed in with other IT tests that test different stuff (like, "can I handle a valid bibframe document, all other variables (such as character set encoding) being controlled?")  Ideally, I'd like to PUT 2049 bytes of /dev/urandom to the Fedora server, and have it say something gently remonstrative and useful to me about why that won't work.
Okay, that makes sense. Are you going to bring in that IT (or set of them) in this ticket, as part of the

No, I would make it separate ticket, more focused on handling character encoding.  I'm inclined to just keep this ticket open to address the failing bibframe tests, and whatever it is we decide to do to make it pass.  The other ticket could be linked to this one, of course.
Okay, but the real point is, I'd rather not change the character encoding in the example. I'd rather get the other piece done and then this ticket will "close itself", if you see what I mean.
The permanent fix for this issue will be addressed in FCREPO-1979.
Ignore the Bibframe test until the larger issue of non-UTF8 character encodings is resolved.

The problem appears to be a character encoding issue: if you remove the inverted exclamation point from the bf:title value of the test bibframe record in the integration test, the test then passes on Windows. Put it back in, and the test fails.

https://github.com/fcrepo4/fcrepo4/blob/master/fcrepo-integration-rdf/src/test/java/org/fcrepo/integration/rdf/BibframeIT.java#L57

I'll look into this more: as far as I can tell, that character is a valid UTF-8 character.

The problem is the default platform encoding:

$ mvn --version
Apache Maven 3.2.3 (33f8c3e1027c3ddde99d3cdebad2656a31e8fdf4; 2014-08-11T15:58:10-05:00)
Maven home: c:\Users\prater.DOIT-R9XFPRF\Projects\Maven
Java version: 1.8.0_73, vendor: Oracle Corporation
Java home: c:\Program Files\Java\jdk1.8.0_73\jre
Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: Cp1252
OS name: "windows 7", version: "6.1", arch: "amd64", family: "dos"

This works:

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Dfile.encoding=UTF8" mvn clean install -rf :fcrepo-integration-rdf

http://javarevisited.blogspot.com/2012/01/get-set-default-character-encoding.html
We shouldn't really ever be using default platform encoding, we should explicitly call out UTF-8 via java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8. He wrote, knowing that he rarely does that.

At the very least, shouldn't the server detect if there's an encoding mismatch, and return something a bit more enlightening than a java.nio.charset.MalformedInputException? I'm thinking it may make more sense to fix this test, then open up an enhancement ticket for later on, to gracefully deal with encoding issues, complete with some sample curl transactions to test the behavior (later to be fleshed out as character encoding integration tests).

Definitely built into the server (the fcrepo-http-api or -commons code, I should think). Everything flowing in after the HTTP machinery should be UTF-8. That's how we get rid of this nonsense once and for all. I think we could do something here with JAX-RS machinery to ensure it.

I take your point about the test in question being about Bibframe, but ironically, library metadata is an oozing, crusty pit full of badly-formed characters washing around in a greasy puddle of XML that lies about its own encoding. It's probably where this kind of problem would first appear, anyway.
